Exosomes are extracellular vesicles sized 30-100 nm, formed in multivesicular endosomes and secreted into extracellular space.
Exosomes carry cytosolic molecules including miRNA, mRNA, proteins, peptides, enzymes, and dsDNA.
Exosome membranes preserve the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, including the glycome and glycocalyx, contributing to immune tolerance.
Surface proteins on exosomes include tetraspanins (CD63, CD81, CD82, CD9, CD86), MHC class I and II, heat-shock proteins, integrins, and complement regulators.
Complement regulatory proteins CD55, CD59, CD46, and CK2 kinase on exosomes inhibit complement activation and membrane attack complex formation.
Exosomes avoid immune recognition and complement-mediated lysis, enabling longer circulation times.
Tumor-derived exosomes transfer oncogenic materials and microRNAs that promote tumor progression, metastasis, and immune evasion.
Exosomes participate in viral infections by delivering viral proteins and RNA, aiding viral replication and pathogenesis.
Exosomes modulate immune responses by antigen presentation, inducing immune tolerance, and regulating T cell apoptosis via FasL.
Provenge®, an FDA-approved dendritic cell-derived exosome vaccine, improves survival in metastatic prostate cancer patients by activating immune responses.
Exosomes can be loaded with therapeutic agents during biogenesis or post-isolation, but loading methods like electroporation may disrupt exosome membranes.
Exosomes have advantages over synthetic nanoparticles including low immunogenicity, natural immune evasion, and ability to carry diverse cargos.
Exosomes are being explored as diagnostic biomarkers in cancer, pulmonary diseases, and metabolic disorders via detection of specific proteins and microRNAs.
Exosome biogenesis involves ESCRT complexes, ALIX, tetraspanins, Rab proteins, and lipid-dependent mechanisms such as ceramide-induced budding.
Exosomes expressing FasL contribute to immune tolerance during pregnancy by inducing apoptosis of activated T cells and modulating regulatory T cells.
Exosomes derived from immune cells can modulate immune responses by stimulating or suppressing T cells.
Exosomes from platelets may inhibit aggregation and thrombosis.
Exosomes are involved in neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Exosomes can induce drug resistance in cancer and neurological diseases by transferring protective molecules.
Clinical trials are ongoing for exosome-based therapies in cancer and inflammatory diseases, with some showing promising results.
